FILED 2026-09-02 02:10 AUSEST by the acting mayor, from the Method reread loop (loops.md
§6), about a decision I had made correctly twenty minutes earlier for a reason the document
does not give.

THE SECTION. loops.md §2, "Routing a finding onto a live worker's file". It offers two
moves. Route-and-note: "message the worker that holds the file, and the fix lands inside the
change that is already open". Queue-and-note: "Sometimes routing is the wrong move
altogether. It widens a deliberately bounded fence mid-flight, which is how a bounded repair
becomes an unbounded one."

THE GAP. The route branch's clause "the change that is already open" reads as DESCRIPTION of
the happy path, not as a PRECONDITION to test - and the queue branch names exactly one
trigger, fence-widening. So a mayor holding a finding whose surface is held by a live agent
WHOSE CHANGE HAS ALREADY MERGED finds neither branch obviously applicable, and the default
pull is to route, because routing is the section's headline move and the agent is right
there and messageable.

WHY THAT FAILS OPEN. Routing into an agent with no open change hands fresh work to a
transient owner with nothing to carry it - which is the precise shape the section's own next
paragraph says evaporates ("the message lives in one agent's transcript, so if that agent
dies, times out, or reasonably declines the extra item ... the finding evaporates"). The
section records that hazard against the AGENT (it may die or decline) and not against the
CHANGE, so a reader who has satisfied himself the agent is alive - which is easy, and which
I had done - reads the warning as discharged.

MEASURED TODAY, and this is what I want on the record because I nearly took the wrong
branch. rf2-7htk7 was reopened by the PR #8963 audit with two concrete findings. The agent
that wrote #8963 was STILL RUNNING and still holding tools/xray/, I had messaged it an hour
earlier, and its PR was MERGED. Route was the reflex; queue was correct. I reached queue by
reasoning from the clause rather than by reading a rule, which is exactly the situation §6
exists to catch.

APPLYING THE DOCUMENT'S OWN DISCHARGING TEST to this finding, since #8962 just installed it:
what would I expect to SEE that is different if this claim were false? A sentence in that
section naming a merged, closed or finished change as a queue trigger, or naming the absence
of an open change at all. Searched the section as a flat string: "already open" and "landed"
are present; "merged", "no open change", "has closed", "finished" and "not open" are all
absent. So the claim is not merely un-refuted, it has a positive check behind it.

PROPOSED - ONE CLAUSE, and it belongs inside the existing route paragraph rather than as a
third branch. Say that routing works BECAUSE there is an open change for the fix to land in,
so that is the thing to check first; where the holder's change has already landed, there is
nothing to route into and the queue branch is the one to take even though no fence is being
widened. Keep both existing branches and both existing reasons exactly as they are - this
adds a second trigger to the queue branch, it does not replace the first. Add no mechanism:
the section says outright that an owner plus one note "does not want to grow past that: no
routing registry, no tracking field, no script", and that binds this repair.

SEQUENCING. docs/the-mayor-method/ is SOLE-TOUCHER hot-zone. rf2-e9z2e is IN FLIGHT on
loops.md §5 right now. This finding is being ROUTED to that worker rather than dispatched -
see the routing note below - which is the section's own preferred move and is available here
precisely because that worker's change IS open, the condition this bead is about. If it does
not land there, this item dispatches on its own once that PR merges.

GATE: python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py plus python -m mkdocs build --strict (exclude_docs
does NOT hide the-mayor-method/). Run mkdocs as "python -m mkdocs" - bare mkdocs returns 127
here, which is NO VERDICT rather than a pass. Neither gate reads prose: verify by hand.

ROUTED 2026-09-02 02:12 AUSEST to the live rf2-e9z2e worker (worktree reaproute-e9z2e,
branch worker/reaproute-e9z2e), which holds docs/the-mayor-method/ under the sole-toucher
rule and whose change is OPEN - the condition this bead is about, which is what makes
routing available here rather than queueing.

WHAT WAS ROUTED: the one-clause repair described above, in full, with the proposed wording
constraints (inside the existing route paragraph, a second queue trigger rather than a
replacement, no mechanism).

WHAT HAPPENS IF IT DOES NOT LAND: the worker was told declining is a fine answer, because
taking it widens a deliberately bounded repair mid-flight. If it declines, or never answers,
or its PR merges without this clause, THIS ITEM DISPATCHES ON ITS OWN once the method
surface frees. The item is the durable owner; the message is not.

ROUTING DID NOT LAND, verified 2026-09-02 02:52 AUSEST at the published head of PR #8966
(worker/reaproute-e9z2e). The PR touches docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md only, and its 19 added
lines carry the rf2-e9z2e repair alone - probes for 'already open', 'landed', 'queue' and
'nothing to route' all return zero across the added lines.

THAT ZERO IS CONTROLLED, not assumed: the same instrument over the same added lines returns
5 hits for 'location', 8 for 'id', 4 for 'sink' and 5 for 'search', which is the rf2-e9z2e
content the PR is FOR. So the instrument reads this diff correctly and the clause is genuinely
absent, rather than the probe being wrong - which is the failure mode a bare zero would have
hidden.

WHY IT DID NOT LAND: the routed message was queued at 02:12 and that agent's transcript has
been byte-identical since ~02:08, across three readings spanning ~24 minutes while a control
agent dispatched in the same window grew continuously. It never took a tool round, so the
message was never delivered. Nothing was declined; nothing was read.

SO THE FALLBACK RECORDED ABOVE IS NOW THE LIVE PATH: this item dispatches on its own once the
method surface frees. It is NOT carried by #8966 and must not be closed against it. The item
was always the durable owner and this is exactly the case that provision was written for.

STILL FENCED: docs/the-mayor-method/ is sole-toucher and #8966 is open against loops.md, so
this waits for #8966 to merge or close - not for the agent.

CORRECTION 2026-09-02 03:34 AUSEST — THE ROUTING DID LAND. The note above ("ROUTING DID NOT
LAND") was true when written and is now false; do not act on it.

WHAT CHANGED: PR #8966's head moved from cdb27a7af2 to 5c4ec7c668 and it now carries TWO
commits, the second being "docs(method): make the open change the precondition routing turns
on, ...". The worker took the routed message after all - it simply had not reached a tool round
when I measured, which is exactly what the earlier note said the byte-identical transcript
meant. The inference from the clock was right about the delivery and wrong about the outcome.

CONSEQUENCE, and it REVERSES the instruction above: this item IS carried by #8966 and SHOULD be
closed against it once that PR merges - on merge evidence, verified against main, not on the
PR's state. It does NOT need its own dispatch.

WHY THIS CORRECTION IS HERE RATHER THAN AN EDIT: the earlier note is the record of a decision
made on the evidence available, and the fallback it set out was the right provision at the time.
Overwriting it would hide that the routing looked dead for half an hour, which is the fact worth
keeping - a routed finding can arrive long after the clock says the agent is gone, so "the
routing did not land" is a claim with a shelf life and wants re-checking at the holder's tip
before it is acted on.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8966, verified on main at adf1271104 (docs(method): make the open change the precondition routing turns on, not scene-setting). Verified by MERGE, not by PR state. One clause inside the existing route paragraph of loops.md section 2, making the open change the precondition routing TURNS ON rather than scene-setting, and adding a second trigger to the queue branch: where the holder's change has already landed there is nothing to route into, so queue even though no fence is being widened. Both existing branches and both existing reasons untouched; no mechanism added, per the section's own 'no routing registry, no tracking field, no script'. ROUTED rather than dispatched, which is the move this item is about - available precisely because the holder's change was open. THE ROUTING TIMELINE IS THE POINT AND IS WORTH KEEPING: the message was queued at 02:12; at 02:48 I recorded on this bead that it had NOT landed, verified against #8966's published head with a controlled zero (probes for the clause absent while probes for the sibling repair's content returned 5, 8, 4 and 5 hits); the worker took it later and the head moved cdb27a7af2 -> 5c4ec7c668. So the instrument was right about DELIVERY and wrong about OUTCOME. The worker read that 02:48 note, recognised it as correct-when-written, took the work because the route-availability condition held, and DELIBERATELY did not claim to close this item in its PR body - naming it, explaining the timeline, and leaving the close to the mayor. That is the right judgement and the reason this close is being made on merge evidence rather than on the PR's claim. Premise verified at source by the worker: 'merged', 'no open change', 'has closed', 'finished' and 'not open' all absent from that section while 'already open' and 'landed' are present, with three section-specific controls confirming the instrument reads the text.

title: WebSocket stale timeout can settle a newer same-ID request
description:
Audit finding from PR #8936 across completeness, correctness, and implementation quality.

The PR correctly makes a live-socket timeout explicit, but the worked and runnable machines correlate a timeout only by `request-id` plus the socket actor id. That rejects timers from an old connection, not an old registration on the same live socket.

At merged commit 23e25e4040:
- `:register-request` stores `[:in-flight request-id]` and schedules `:ws/request-timeout` carrying only that id and `:source-socket-id`.
- `:clear-request` looks up whichever entry currently occupies that id, removes it, and now dispatches its reply-event a local `:ws/timeout`.
- The spec permits any `=`-comparable id and explicitly recommends reusable per-feature vectors such as `[:feature/load slug]`; uniqueness for a socket lifetime is not a contract.

Concrete failure: request A with id R completes; request B reuses R on the same still-live socket before A's uncancelled deadline; A's timer passes `:current-socket?`, deletes B, and fires B's callback with a premature timeout. Registering B while A is still pending also overwrites A's callback without settling it. Both violate the page's new exactly-once/terminal-outcome promise.

Keep the repair local to the WebSocket pattern: correlate scheduled timeouts to the specific registration they came from and state the duplicate-in-flight policy. Do not build a generic timer-cancellation layer or managed WebSocket abstraction.
acceptance_criteria: A timeout or wire reply can settle only the exact in-flight registration it belongs to; an uncancelled timeout from an earlier same-ID request on the same socket cannot clear or notify a later request. Concurrent duplicate IDs have an explicit policy that does not strand a displaced caller. The spec, runnable example, schema if needed, and focused tests agree, while preserving socket-epoch rejection and the existing local/server provenance shapes. No generic cancellation facility or new public WebSocket abstraction.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8946 (2026-09-02) — REOPENED BECAUSE WIRE REPLIES STILL CORRELATE TO THE REUSED ID, NOT THE REGISTRATION.

The timeout half is sound: `:own-request-timeout?` checks both socket epoch and registration token. The same token never reaches the wire-reply path, though:

- `:register-request` still sends `(assoc body :request-id request-id)` with no registration discriminator.
- `ReplyMessage` carries only `:request-id`.
- `:receive-message` looks up and removes whichever entry currently occupies `[:in-flight (:request-id body)]`, without a token check.

Concrete failure: A is pending under `R`; B re-registers `R`, locally superseding A, and both requests are now on the wire with the identical correlation value. When A's server reply arrives first, `:receive-message` finds B's slot, removes it, and fires B's callback with A's body. B's actual reply later becomes unsolicited. The callback count can remain exactly once while the reply is attached to the wrong registration—the more fundamental correlation failure.

This directly contradicts this bead's acceptance criterion: "A timeout or wire reply can settle only the exact in-flight registration it belongs to." The merged spec instead disclaims which server reply answers which registration and says the reply settles whichever registration holds the slot; that narrows the required end state rather than satisfying it. The two new tests use `:silent-no-echo`, so neither injects A's wire reply after B takes the slot and the missing fence is unobserved.

Completeness: the registration identity protects deadlines only. Correctness: last-write-wins plus an unchanged wire id can deliver stale data as B's successful response. Implementation quality: an explicitly ambiguous request/reply contract is a sharp edge in the recommended reusable-id pattern, and the focused tests avoid the ambiguous branch.

Minimal outcome: preserve exact wire correlation either by ensuring two registrations with one wire id are never concurrently outstanding (for example, reject/serialize the newcomer) or by putting a registration discriminator on the wire and requiring it back; add the A-reply-after-B-registration regression. Keep this local to the example—no managed-WebSocket abstraction or generic cancellation layer.

Duplicate search: `rf2-tb442` owns this exact same-id registration-correlation contract and already names wire replies in its acceptance criteria, so it is reopened rather than duplicated.
close_reason:
Second pass (audit PR #8946), PR #8959. The reopen was about the WIRE-REPLY half of the correlation, and that is what this addressed: :register-request now stamps the registration :token onto the outbound frame as :request-token beside :request-id, schema/ReplyMessage REQUIRES it echoed back, and :receive-message settles the [:in-flight rid] slot only while the echoed token is still the slot's token. A mismatch is treated as an unsolicited reply (nothing cleared, no :reply-event fired, frame still reaches the inbox), not an error. Duplicate-in-flight policy (last-write-wins, displaced caller settled :ws/superseded) is unchanged; the displaced registration now leaves two inert leftovers rather than one -- its armed timer and the reply its request will still draw from the server.

REGRESSION PROVING A WIRE REPLY CAN NO LONGER SETTLE A LATER SAME-ID REGISTRATION: deftest websocket-wire-reply-cannot-settle-a-later-same-id-registration in implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs. A registers under the reusable id [:feature/load "gamma"] and stays pending; B re-registers the same id (A settled :ws/superseded, A's request still on the wire); A's SERVER reply then arrives carrying A's token. Asserted: the slot still holds B's token, B's callback count is still 1, and A's reply reaches the inbox as an unsolicited vetted frame -- then B's own reply settles B with B's OWN body and B's token. RED BEFORE / GREEN AFTER measured: with :receive-message's token check reverted to (get-in data [:in-flight rid]) and everything else left in place, the focused suite returned captured exit 1 with 4 failures, ALL in that test, on the same 29 tests / 240 assertions -- including 'expected (= {:type :request :tag "B"} (:echo outcome)) / actual (not (= {:type :request :tag "B"} {:type :request :tag "A"}))', which is the defect in one row: B's caller handed A's body as its answer. Restored (verified by git blob hash against the committed object), recompiled, re-run: captured exit 0.

Gates, captured exit codes from the runner: node-test compile 0 (1877 files, 0 warnings); node out/node-test.js 0 (11197 tests, 55483 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors); focused websocket ns 0 (29 tests, 240 assertions); check_doc_slugs.py 0; check_readme_links.py --ci 0. Both link gates exercised against a planted broken target first and returned exit 1 naming the planted file and line, so their greens are measured rather than silent.

EP-0011 CANARY HELD. The app-level/no-uniform-envelope boundary is intact: :request-token is an ordinary unqualified app key on the app's own wire frame, not :work/id or :rf/reply-to. The five 'app-level reply carries no EP-0011 ...' assertions pass, and they are live -- planting the five envelope keys onto the reply body reds all five. ServerReplyOutcome is also a :closed map, so envelope vocabulary on this path is a schema rejection as well.

WIRE COMPATIBILITY, stated because the outbound body changed: a server that ignores :request-token echoes only :request-id, its reply then fails the closed ReplyMessage arm, and the frame takes :refuse-frame -- nothing in the connection moves, the slot is not cleared, no callback fires, and the ingress mints the canonical :rf.error/schema-validation-failure naming the missing key on the very first reply; the request then settles on its own deadline with the documented {:origin :ws/local :ok false :error :ws/timeout}. So it degrades to a loud, terminal, documented outcome, never to silence and never to wrong data. Admitting an untokened reply and correlating by id would have restored the exact ambiguity the field removes. The escape hatch is documented in ReplyMessage's docstring and Pattern-WebSocket item 6: an app whose server cannot echo the field drops it from BOTH ReplyMessage and :register-request and then owes its ids uniqueness for the socket's lifetime. A new boundary case pins this -- a reply omitting only :request-token is refused and the in-flight slot survives it.

Scope kept local to the WebSocket pattern per the bead: one wire field, one required schema entry, one equality check, plus spec/example/skill/README prose. No managed-WebSocket abstraction, no generic correlation or cancellation layer, no new public surface.

SPEC CHANGE OF NOTE: Pattern-WebSocket item 6 previously DISCLAIMED this ('the wire reply settles whichever registration holds the slot'), which narrowed the acceptance criterion rather than meeting it. That disclaimer is removed and item 6 is restructured around both settling paths, with a new anti-pattern for fixing the timer and leaving the reply.

ADJACENT FINDING, not fixed here, may deserve a follow-up bead: the test fixture's register-all! re-declares the two ingress event-handler BODIES inline and runs on every test, so those bodies -- not the example's -- are what the suite exercises. Measured: a fault planted in websocket.messages' :ws.app/request-reply body left the suite fully green. Where the fixture points at an example VAR instead (connection machine, socket actor, schemas, mock transport) the example's own code genuinely is under test and a planted fault reds immediately; everything this PR changes substantively falls in that second group. The fixture docstring now records the distinction.

title: mayor method: frozen clocks are ambiguous, not a signature of imminent completion
description:
OPERATIONAL, filed by the mayor 2026-09-01 15:10 AUSEST for Mike's call. Not a code defect.

SYMPTOM. Three background workers report 'running' in the agent listing while every independent signal says they are idle:
  - a95b2faa (rf2-ni0ko, PR #8872): last commit 2h ago, worktree clean, local tip == remote tip, no reply to a direct message sent ~30 min ago.
  - a458d57b (rf2-g1m2q, PR #8876): last commit 79 min ago, no file write since 13:51, worktree clean, tip == remote, no reply to a direct message.
  - abed3ebfd (rf2-j3tud fix worker): its PR MERGED two hours ago and its remote branch was deleted; zero unmerged patches; no write for 80+ min; no reply to a stop-and-report sent ~50 min ago.

COST, and it is not just slots. PR #8876 reads 85 checks / 0 non-terminal / 0 failing — the current band exactly. It clears every clause of the merge criterion EXCEPT the draft flag, which only its author can flip. PR #8872 is complete too but computed against the pre-#8868 matrix (84), so it needs a rebase as well as a ready mark. So two finished changes are stranded behind an interlock whose protected party may no longer exist, and the effective fleet is 3 of 6.

WHY THE MAYOR HAS NOT ACTED. Three candidate remedies, each reserved:
  (a) Flip the draft flag myself. The interlock exists so the merge loop cannot land a change out from under a live worker; overriding it on an INFERENCE that the worker is dead is exactly the proxy the reaping rules exist to forbid, one surface over.
  (b) Stop the agents (TaskStop), which would establish they are not live and discharge (a) honestly — but destroys any unwritten report, and the reports are the outstanding deliverable.
  (c) Dispatch around them to keep 6 ACTIVE. Done once already this session and it worked, but it grows the registered-agent count without bound if agents keep going quiet, and it is the wrong move if the cause is machine contention.

DIAGNOSIS IS UNRESOLVED and that is why this is filed rather than fixed. The competing explanation is loops.md section 2's wedge: a heavyweight gate that stalls with no progress, no exit file and no error, which would also explain why messages are not drained (they land at the receiver's next tool round, and a wedged tool call never reaches one). Machine reads 58 chrome and 11 node processes against 1 java — real browser-lane activity, but attributable to the three ACTIVE workers, so it neither confirms nor refutes the wedge.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: whether the harness's 'running' state distinguishes a live turn from an agent stuck in a hung tool call, and whether there is a liveness probe cheaper than a message that a wedged agent cannot answer.
acceptance_criteria:
- Both method pages describe frozen tip/fetch/write/message observations as non-discriminating: compatible with long foreground work/final hygiene and also with a stopped or wedged worker, never a positive signature of either state.
- A direct live-progress signal remains preferred; without one, the guidance is to declare a window and re-read without acting on the clocks alone.
- The five-worker/sixth-worker outcome count is stated consistently across both pages and matches the recorded incident.
- The fix-dispatch re-draft/verify rule and conservative never-flip-on-inference rule remain intact; no dashboard or new activity sweep.
notes:
METHOD REREAD 2026-09-01 15:16:13 AUSEST: the GENERAL rule this incident exposed is now written up in PR #8885 — docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md, section 'Publishing the change'. It records that the draft interlock fails in BOTH directions (stale-open on a fix dispatch, stuck-closed on a silent author), says explicitly not to flip the flag on an inference, and settles the resolution as a read rather than an inference: the agent's own report, or the operator's decision to stop the agent, which settles liveness by making it false.

THIS ITEM IS NOT THEREBY CLOSED. The doc change captures the rule; the operator question it names is still open and still Mike's — which of the three remedies to take here, and whether the harness's 'running' state can distinguish a live turn from an agent stuck in a hung tool call. Two finished changes remain stranded meanwhile.
UPDATE 2026-09-01 15:49 AUSEST — the problem has GROWN in two directions, and neither was visible when this was filed.

(1) FOUR dormant, not three. ab64ac300 (rf2-k2d2t, PR #8882) has joined them: its PR has carried two clj-kondo failures untouched for over an hour, which is the same shape as the others — registered running, nothing moving. Registered agents now number NINE against five genuinely active.

(2) IT HAS PROPAGATED INTO THE BACKLOG. Two open beads are now fenced behind the two stranded DRAFTS, so the cost is no longer just the stuck changes:
  - rf2-yasvj waits on PR #8876 (classifier-skills) merging.
  - rf2-0g60h waits on PR #8872 (ws-fatal) merging.
Neither can be dispatched, and neither fence can clear by any action available to me, because the merge criterion refuses a draft and only the author can lift that flag. A fence whose release condition is held by an agent that has stopped is not a queue; it is a dead end.

SALVAGE TEST RUN, and the answer is reassuring: NOTHING is at risk. ws-fatal, classifier-skills and urldecode all read local tip == remote tip, and routing-encoding shows no remote ref only because its branch was deleted on merge — git cherry reports zero unmerged patches against main, so its work is contained there. Every dormant agent has its work either merged or pushed. What is stranded is the READY MARK and the REPORTS, not the code.

That bounds the decision usefully: stopping these agents would cost the unwritten reports and nothing else. It does not make the call for you, but the downside is now measured rather than feared.
THE COST IS NOW A TRACKER LIE, 2026-09-01 15:55 AUSEST. Both stranded drafts have CLOSED beads whose work is NOT on main — rf2-g1m2q (PR #8876) and rf2-ni0ko (PR #8872) each read CLOSED while git cherry reports one patch with no upstream equivalent.

This is the documented consequence of beads closing on PR-OPEN rather than on merge, which is normally benign because changes merge within the hour. Here two of them cannot merge at all, so the tracker permanently asserts work the trunk does not have.

AND IT IS INVISIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION. The backlog reread reads OPEN items; nothing re-reads a closed one. So these two will not surface in any loop again: they are not a closure that REVERTED (that at least reappears in the open list), they are a closure that was never true. If those PRs are eventually abandoned, two closed beads silently describe absent work and the next person to touch that surface finds the defect still there with a closed item saying it was fixed.

NOTE THE SYMMETRY, because it is exactly inverted from the finding merged this session as PR #8888. That addition taught the backlog loop to catch an OPEN item that is already DONE. This is a CLOSED item that is UNDONE. Both are the tracker disagreeing with the tree; only one direction is now covered, and the uncovered direction is the one no loop reads. Raised for the next method-reread rather than acted on here.

NOTHING IS LOST EITHER WAY: both branches are pushed, so the code survives regardless of what is decided about the agents.
NEGATIVE RESULT 2026-09-01 16:20 AUSEST — MESSAGING DOES NOT REACH THESE AGENTS, and this rules out the most comfortable explanation.

Three direct messages have now gone to dormant agents (a458d57b, a95b2faa, a861d3726). ZERO replies. The third is the informative one: a861d3726 was messaged within MINUTES of its PR merging, proactively, precisely to stop it becoming another two-hour zombie — while it was presumably still mid-turn and had every reason to answer. It has now been running 52 minutes since, has not replied, and is dormant number five.

WHAT THAT ELIMINATES: "the message arrived after the agent had already stopped" was the kind explanation, and it does not survive this. The message was early, the agent was fresh, and nothing came back.

WHY IT MATTERS TO THE METHOD RATHER THAN JUST TO THIS BOARD: the stranded sweep leans on message-first as its liveness discriminator — send one, because a reply distinguishes alive from finished where a transcript cannot. Against this failure that discriminator is not merely slow, it is INOPERATIVE. A message queues for delivery at the receiver a tool round, and an agent that never reaches another tool round never drains it. So the one probe the method offers is exactly the probe this condition defeats, and its silence is indistinguishable from an agent that is busy working.

The practical consequence for anyone reading this later: do not spend further messages on an agent already showing the pattern (registered running, tip unmoved, no writes, work pushed). One is worth sending. The second and third are not, and I sent them.

FLEET STATE: 11 registered, 6 genuinely active, 5 dormant. The ceiling is not yet binding because idle agents contend for nothing, but the registered set now grows monotonically.

--- MAYOR MEASUREMENT 2026-09-01 16:45 AUSEST ---

The dormant set has grown from three to FIVE, and the two drafts it strands are now measured rather than described:

  PR #8876 (worker/classifier-skills-g1m2q, rf2-g1m2q): 85 checks, 0 non-terminal, 0 failing.
    FULLY GREEN AT BAND. It is blocked by nothing except the draft flag its author never unset.
    Last updated 03:58Z; measured at 06:45Z, so roughly 2h45m stranded.
  PR #8872 (worker/ws-fatal-ni0ko, rf2-ni0ko): 84 checks, 0 non-terminal, 0 failing.
    Green, but at band-minus-one -- it branched before the job that moved the band to 85 landed,
    so clause 5 needs a rebase before it can be judged. That rebase is work no live agent will do.

DOWNSTREAM COST, enumerated: four ready beads are fenced behind those two changes.
  Behind #8876: rf2-yasvj (retire the stale "skills_structural does not yet fire" caveats) and
                rf2-qxg24 (surface-review conformance-security classifier pair).
  Behind #8872: rf2-0g60h (spec/Pattern-WebSocket worked example still teaches the leak).
  Plus rf2-g1m2q and rf2-ni0ko themselves read CLOSED while their work is not on main.

WHY THE MAYOR HAS NOT ACTED: the publishing section of the dispatch template rules that a stuck-CLOSED
draft is NOT settled by flipping the flag on an inference -- "it looks done" is the same proxy the
reaping rules refuse. It is settled by a read: the agents own report, or the operators decision to stop
that agent, which settles liveness by making it false. Neither has arrived, so both changes wait.

NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE ONE PROBE THE METHOD OFFERS: three direct messages to dormant agents have produced
zero replies. The most recent was sent PROACTIVELY within minutes of that agents PR merging, while it was
presumably still mid-turn -- which eliminates "the message arrived too late" as the explanation. A message
queues for the receivers next tool round, and an agent that never reaches another tool round never drains
it. So message-first, the stranded sweeps liveness discriminator, is INOPERATIVE against this failure
rather than merely slow, and its silence is indistinguishable from an agent that is busy working.
Practical advice: one message is worth sending; the second and third are not.

NOTHING IS AT RISK. Every dormant agents work is merged or pushed. What accumulates is the registered
agent set, two finished changes, and four fenced beads.

--- STRANDED SWEEP 2026-09-01 16:49 AUSEST: the harness liveness probe is defeated by this failure ---

Ran the full loops.md ss4 sweep from the worktrees. Result: NOTHING TO SALVAGE, NOTHING TO REDISPATCH.
All five dormant worktrees have local HEAD == origin HEAD and clean status; routing-encoding has no
origin branch at all but git cherry against main returns "-", i.e. its commit is already patch-equivalent
on the trunk. So step 3 of the sweep has no work in it: every commit is durable, three of the five are
already merged.

CLOCKS, run properly rather than reasserted:
  fetch-head read twice, 16:46:49 and 16:49:06 (2m17s apart), per-worktree copy:
    ws-fatal 14:00:59 frozen | classifier-skills 13:50:48 frozen | routing-encoding 13:45:31 frozen
    urldecode 14:40:15 frozen | ssr-form2 15:35:03 frozen
    CONTROL, same instrument, same two reads: runrecipes moved 16:26:17 -> 16:47:30 with its tip
    advancing 3a52bc795c -> a776ebb49f. So the instrument works and the stillness is real, which a
    single read could never have established.
  write clock at TWO spans (5 min and 60 min) on the three oldest: all zero at both. Their creation
  times are 12:53, 13:18 and 13:31, so the 60-minute span sits well inside the trees own age and the
  zero is a genuine no-writes rather than the checkout-age artefact the method warns about.

THE FINDING THAT IS NEW, AND IT IS ABOUT THE SWEEP ITSELF:

loops.md ss4 step 3 endorses asking the harness whether an agent is RUNNING, and calls it "decisive in
one direction: an agent under an exhausted allowance dies within seconds of being resumed, so minutes of
running is positive evidence the allowance came back."

That reading does not survive THIS failure mode. All five of these agents report RUNNING -- for between
1h11m and 3h01m -- while every other clock says idle and their trees say finished. So "running" is
positive evidence of life ONLY in the narrow post-resume context the method describes, where the
alternative is near-instant death. Read generally, which is how the rule is written, it inverts: it
becomes the single most reassuring signal on the board and it IS the symptom.

That matters because the probe is cheap and the method presents it as the fast path -- a mayor reaching
for it first, as designed, gets told all five are alive and stops sweeping. The per-worktree fetch-head
clock read twice is what actually discriminated here, and it is the slower, less obvious instrument.

NOT FIXING THE DOCUMENT FROM THIS LOOP -- the posture loop flags drift, the method-reread loop repairs
the text. Recorded here so the repair has its measurement when that loop next runs.

--- COUNT CORRECTION + NEW ARRIVAL 2026-09-01 17:08 AUSEST ---

CORRECTION TO MY 16:45 NOTE. That note said "four ready beads are fenced behind those two changes" and
then enumerated THREE (rf2-yasvj, rf2-qxg24 behind #8876; rf2-0g60h behind #8872). The count and its
breakdown disagreed. The breakdown was right and the count was wrong: it was three, not four. Stating
it plainly because the number is the thing an operator would act on, and because a total that does not
match its own list is exactly the error I keep a note about.

IT IS NOW GENUINELY FOUR, by arrival rather than by recount. rf2-bbe91 (P3, wire the MIG-23 cold-start
fixture into the skills-structural CI job) modifies .github/workflows/test.yml, and its own description
says so: "Hot-zone: touches .github/workflows/test.yml -- sequence accordingly." #8876 modifies the
SAME job in the SAME file, so bbe91 cannot be dispatched while #8876 sits unmerged.

CURRENT FENCED SET, enumerated and counted from that enumeration:
  Behind #8876 (85 checks, 0 non-terminal, 0 failing -- fully green at band, author dormant ~3h):
    rf2-yasvj, rf2-qxg24, rf2-bbe91   = 3
  Behind #8872 (84 checks, green but band-minus-one, needs a rebase no live agent will do):
    rf2-0g60h                          = 1
  TOTAL FENCED READY BEADS = 4
  Plus rf2-g1m2q and rf2-ni0ko, which read CLOSED while their work is not on main.

THE TREND IS THE POINT, not the number. Two of these four did not exist when the drafts stranded; they
arrived afterwards and landed on the same hot file. A stranded change in a hot-zone file does not hold a
fixed queue -- it ACCRETES one, because every later item touching that file must sequence behind it. So
the cost of this hold grows on its own without anything new going wrong.

A SIXTH INSTANCE MAY BE FORMING. PR #8892 (worker/issuebody-2zkrz) has been green at band for about
25 minutes and remains a draft; its worktree tip has not moved and its fetch-head clock has been frozen
at 16:23:12 for 43 minutes, measured twice. I am NOT recording it as stranded: the method names exactly
this shape -- green at band, clean tree, still tip, still draft -- as the most convincing FALSE signature,
because a worker on attempt three of a local gate presents identically. One status message sent, which is
the whole budget my earlier negative result allows. Recorded so the next tick can compare rather than
re-derive.

=== MAYOR RETRACTION 2026-09-01 17:14 AUSEST: THIS BEAD PREMISE IS LARGELY WRONG ===

FOUR OF THE FIVE AGENTS I CLASSIFIED AS DORMANT HAVE NOW COMPLETED, ALIVE, WITH FULL REPORTS.
Within about fifteen minutes of my last note:
  a458d57b classifier-skills  ran 3h33m, delivered PR #8876 (now MERGED)
  abed3ebfd routing-encoding  ran 3h25m, delivered a refutation of the mayors own flake hypothesis
  a861d3726 ssr-form2         ran 1h42m, delivered, and corrected an error in its brief
  adb6ce96  issuebody         delivered PR #8892 (now MERGED)
  a7002d8d  runrecipes        delivered PR #8894
Only ab64ac300 (urldecode) and a95b2faa (ws-fatal) remain unexplained, and both may yet complete.

THE MESSAGE-FIRST NEGATIVE RESULT IS RETRACTED IN FULL. I recorded that message-first was
"INOPERATIVE rather than merely slow" against this failure, on three unanswered messages. issuebody
answered mine directly and its opening words settle it: "was my last act; I was on final hygiene when
you pinged -- no gate was running, nothing was stuck." Messages DO arrive. The earlier silences were
exactly what the mechanism predicts -- a message queues for the receivers next tool round, and a worker
three hours into foreground gates reaches one rarely -- but I converted "slow" into "inoperative",
which is a different and much stronger claim, and it was not supported.

WHAT I ACTUALLY MEASURED WAS RIGHT; THE CONCLUSION DRAWN FROM IT WAS WRONG. The frozen fetch-head
clocks, the zero writes at two spans, the unmoved tips -- every one of those readings was accurate.
They are also the EXPECTED readings for a healthy worker inside a long foreground gate, which is what
these were. A worker running gates writes nothing, commits nothing and fetches nothing for as long as
the gate runs, and these gates ran for hours.

THE METHOD ALREADY SAID SO AND I UNDER-WEIGHTED IT. loops.md ss4: "An unchanged tip says nothing on
its own -- a worker inside a long gate commits nothing by design, so a still tip is the EXPECTED
reading for the commonest healthy state." And on the exact shape I kept reporting: "The most convincing
false signature ... a change fully green at the band, a clean worktree, a tip commit some minutes old,
and the change still a DRAFT ... a worker presenting exactly so was on attempt three of its local
gate." I quoted that passage in the same session in which I called five agents dormant.

THE ONE THING THAT WENT RIGHT, AND IT IS THE METHODS DOING RATHER THAN MINE: I never acted on the
wrong reading. No draft flag flipped on an inference, no redispatch, no salvage-and-reopen, no
worktree reaped. ss4 step 3 requires no live task AND no tip movement before acting, and the
publishing section forbids flipping a draft flag on "it looks done". Both held, so a three-hour
misdiagnosis cost nothing but my own reporting. That asymmetry -- "the error is cheap in one direction
only, and it favours waiting" -- is the rule that saved this, and it is worth more than the diagnosis
was.

CORRECTED STATUS OF THIS BEAD: the fenced-bead cost I enumerated is now largely discharged. #8876 is
MERGED, which releases rf2-yasvj, rf2-qxg24 and rf2-bbe91. #8892 is MERGED. What remains is two agents
(urldecode, ws-fatal) still registered running, and #8872 still a draft at band-minus-one needing a
rebase. That is a much smaller claim than this beads title makes, and the title should be retitled or
the bead closed once those two resolve. I am NOT closing it yet: two unexplained agents is not zero,
and closing on a correction would be the same over-reach in the opposite direction.

WHAT SHOULD CHANGE IN MY PRACTICE: a long-running worker is the DEFAULT explanation for a still tree,
not the exotic one. Before reporting an agent dormant, state how long its brief plausibly takes and
whether the gates it was given run for hours. Three of these five were dispatched with heavy
browser/CLJS suites; the arithmetic was available and I did not do it.
AUDIT PR #8885: UPDATED. The method text landed a real stale-OPEN diagnosis but does not complete either direction of the interlock, and its stuck-CLOSED “measurement” was invalidated after merge by this bead's own later evidence. Four of the five supposedly idle workers completed alive with full reports; the frozen tips/clean trees/no writes were expected while long foreground gates ran, and message-first was slow rather than inoperative. `dispatch-prompt-template.md` still presents that retracted incident as a measured failure. Meanwhile the stale-OPEN section says a fix dispatch inherits a ready flag but gives no enforced action that restores the guard; `loops.md` still says the draft interlock costs the merge loop nothing to remember and its fix-worker branch never re-drafts the existing change. Minimal completion: when dispatching a fix worker onto an existing ready PR, synchronously convert it back to draft and verify that state before work begins; the fix worker marks it ready last. Recast/remove the false stuck-CLOSED measurement, retain the conservative stop/report rule for a genuinely silent author, and update the contradictory `loops.md` sibling. No liveness dashboard or per-merge activity sweep.
AUDIT PR #8925: REOPENED. Completeness is strong on the stale-OPEN half: fix dispatches now re-draft and verify the existing change, and loops.md carries the exception. The stuck-CLOSED correction, however, replaces one unsupported inference with its inverse. Both pages first say a dead/wedged worker and a healthy worker in a long gate or final hygiene produce the same frozen tip/fetch/write/message observations, then call frozen-across-readings “the signature of a run about to report.” A pattern explicitly shared by both states cannot identify either one, and “about to” is not supported by hour-long freezes. The two pages also narrate the evidence differently: dispatch-prompt-template records four of five plus a sixth, while loops.md says all five plus the sixth completed. Minimal completion: call the clocks ambiguous/compatible with healthy foreground work, preserve the direct-status-first and wait/re-read rule, and state one sourced outcome count. No liveness dashboard or new sweep.
AUDIT PR #8928: REOPENED exact owner; no duplicate. Completeness and implementation quality are strong: the re-draft instruction now sits at the fix-dispatch action, and the added-line scan no longer claims to settle a case. The frozen-clock conclusion is correctly recast as ambiguous, but the replacement evidence count is still wrong. The source measurement explicitly enumerates five dormant workers: classifier-skills, routing-encoding, ssr-form2, urldecode, and ws-fatal. Only the first three completed; urldecode and ws-fatal remained unexplained. PR #8892 was then recorded as a sixth possible instance and completed, making four of six alive with two unexplained. runrecipes was the moving live CONTROL, not a dormant case, so its later completion cannot make the count five of six. Both edited pages now promote that control into the numerator and say the remaining one was unexplained, contradicting the source's two unexplained workers. Minimal correction: state four of six alive and two unexplained (or avoid a ratio and name the outcomes) in both pages. Preserve the ambiguity guidance, asymmetric-cost wait rule, re-draft placement, and triage wording; no new mechanism or broader method edit.
close_reason: Fixed by PR #8931 (merged 2026-09-01), third and final round on this item. The audit of PR #8928 was right on both counts: the corrected text still quoted a ratio, and that ratio promoted a live CONTROL into the numerator — runrecipes was the moving worker the measurement rested on, not a dormant case — while also understating the unexplained cases. Both pages now NAME THE OUTCOMES instead of reducing them to a ratio: five workers were called dormant, three completed alive, two were never explained either way, and a later sixth also completed; the control is excluded explicitly, with a sentence saying a live control is not a completion and that folding it in is how the count was first written down wrong. The two unexplained workers are now stated as precisely why the reading is ambiguous rather than merely mistaken. Ambiguity guidance, the asymmetric-cost wait rule, the re-draft placement and the triage wording are all preserved unchanged. No new mechanism. Verified after merge: the wrong phrasing returns 0 on both files case-insensitively, against a control term returning 2.

title: bug(examples): Linearlite classifies its simulated 503 as a transport failure
description:
## Scope

Correct the executable failure contract in `examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite/core.cljs` and pin it in the existing `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/linearlite_example_cljs_test.cljs` composition suite. This is the Linearlite demo backend's armed "Fail the next write" path only; the managed-HTTP and mutation runtimes are behaving according to their published contracts.

## Correctness finding

Linearlite says its armed demo backend answers the next write with HTTP 503, but it calls the direct `:rf.http/managed-canned-failure` effect with the failure under `:failure`. That effect's locked args contract is top-level `:kind` plus `:tags`; it ignores `:failure` and therefore defaults to `{:kind :rf.http/transport}`. The mutation still receives `:status :error`, so rollback visibly works and masks the incorrect failure classification.

## Evidence

- `examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite/core.cljs:365-373` builds `{:kind :rf.http/http-5xx :status 503 :message ...}` and passes it as `:failure` to the registered canned-failure handler.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/test_support.cljc:184-208` reads only top-level `:kind` and `:tags`, defaulting them to `:rf.http/transport` and `{}`. `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:1092-1097`, `spec/API.md:398`, and `docs/api/re-frame.http.md:321-336` publish that same shape.
- A JVM probe of the real canned handler with Linearlite's args produced `[:settle {:status :error, :error {:kind :rf.http/transport}}]`. The positive control using top-level `:kind :rf.http/http-5xx` and `:tags {:status 503 :message "simulated"}` produced `[:settle {:status :error, :error {:status 503, :message "simulated", :kind :rf.http/http-5xx}}]`.
- The example repeatedly promises a 503 in `core.cljs` (namespace narrative and backend comments) and `README.md:67-71,126-130`.
- The existing example suite explicitly says it bypasses the example's fail-next-write seam (`linearlite_example_cljs_test.cljs:23-32`) and manually injects a correctly classified 5xx failure at lines 312-350. It proves generic mutation rollback, not the runnable backend that users execute.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Invoke the real `re-frame.http.test-support/emit-canned-failure!` handler with a stamped frame, a `:reply-to`, and the same args shape Linearlite supplies: `{:failure {:kind :rf.http/http-5xx :status 503 :message "simulated"}}`; capture the late-bound router dispatch.
2. Observe the reply is `{:status :error :error {:kind :rf.http/transport}}`: the intended kind, status, and message were discarded.
3. Repeat with the published direct-effect shape `{:kind :rf.http/http-5xx :tags {:status 503 :message "simulated"}}`.
4. Observe the control reply retains `{:kind :rf.http/http-5xx :status 503 :message "simulated"}` under `:error`.

## Failure scenario / invariant

A programmer runs the example, arms "Fail the next write", and executes a mutation. The optimistic board change correctly rolls back, but `[:rf/mutation {:instance ...}]` stores a transport failure with no HTTP status rather than the promised `:rf.http/http-5xx` / 503 failure. Any Xray inspection, response middleware, or copied application branch over the documented closed HTTP failure taxonomy observes a false cause. The runnable example's invariant is: an armed write must settle through the same canonical 503 envelope the example says it synthesises, while retaining the visible optimistic-apply -> rollback arc.

## Recommended minimal fix

Pass the canned-failure effect its existing public shape directly: keep `:after-ms`, set top-level `:kind :rf.http/http-5xx`, and put `:status 503` plus the message in top-level `:tags`. Add one focused test through the actual registered Linearlite demo stub instead of another hand-built failure reply. Do not add support for the erroneous `:failure` alias to managed HTTP; this is pre-alpha and one call site should conform to the one existing contract.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A focused CLJS test drives the actual registered `:linearlite.demo/http-stub` failure path (not the suite's capturing transport and not a manually appended failure reply): it loads a board, arms `:linearlite/set-fail-next-write`, and dispatches one real example write.
- Non-vacuity: before the deferred reply settles, the test proves the write request reached the demo stub and the board contains the optimistic change; after settle, it proves the board equals its exact pre-write value and the mutation instance is terminal `:error` with `:optimistic? false`.
- The same test asserts the stored public mutation `:error` carries `:kind :rf.http/http-5xx`, `:status 503`, and the demo message, and asserts the one-shot flag was disarmed. It must fail against the current `:rf.http/transport` result.
- Positive control: an otherwise equivalent unarmed write through the same actual demo stub settles `:success` and commits, proving the test is selecting the armed branch rather than passing because every request fails or no reply ran.
- The existing create, retitle, and status optimistic apply/commit/rollback assertions remain green; no live network is contacted.
- From `implementation/`, `npm run test:cljs -- --test=re-frame.linearlite-example-cljs-test` passes with a non-zero test/assertion count, and `npm run test:examples-compile` still compiles `examples/linearlite`.

## Non-goals

- Changing the managed-HTTP canned-failure contract, accepting compatibility aliases, or changing failure taxonomy.
- Refactoring mutation rollback, optimistic conflict policy, the demo board, routing, mount code, or the 220 ms illustrative delay.
- Adding a browser automation suite or revising the separate capability README launch instructions.
- Generalising the demo backend or adding production transport behavior.

## Related / duplicate search

All-status title, description, and notes searches covered `linearlite`, `fail next`, `fail-next-write`, `managed-canned-failure`, `canned failure`, `HTTP 503`, `http-5xx`, `rollback seam`, `generic transport`, `simulated server failure`, `failure stub`, `failure envelope`, and `failure taxonomy`. No duplicate was found. `rf2-ujdn0` concerns stale capability README launch commands only; it does not touch Linearlite runtime behavior. `rf2-lddbk` concerns successful live-response metadata through HTTP `:after` middleware, not canned failure classification. `rf2-hic-027` mentions a rollback seam on an unrelated Hicasso test facade.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A focused CLJS test uses the actual `:linearlite.demo/http-stub`, arms fail-next-write, proves an optimistic change exists before settle, then proves exact rollback, one-shot disarm, and mutation error `{:kind :rf.http/http-5xx :status 503 ...}` after settle.
2. An unarmed control through the same stub succeeds and commits; both arms prove requests/replies actually ran.
3. `npm run test:cljs -- --test=re-frame.linearlite-example-cljs-test` reports non-zero tests/assertions and passes; `npm run test:examples-compile` still compiles `examples/linearlite`.
4. No managed-HTTP alias or unrelated runtime/refactor work is introduced.
close_reason: Landed by PR #8845 (merged 2026-09-01T02:51:20Z), commits 9ddeac52ba 'fix(examples/linearlite): classify the armed demo 503 per the canned-failure contract' and 58d8ac27b3 'test(linearlite): pin the armed demo backend's 503 classification at the stub seam' — both verified present on origin/main. The bead was left in_progress because its worker did not survive to close it; the work itself is complete and merged.

title: pair-mcp: retire the progress-stream subsystem (33 -> 29 tools)
description:
## Scope

Make live observation fit an ordinary programmer+AI tool turn. Retire Pair-MCP's progress-notification streaming subsystem: the public `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `list-streams`, and `get-stream-controls` tools; their server/runtime queue, polling, accounting, and launch-control machinery; and their schema, manifest, test, spec, skill, and conformance carriers. Establish the already-shipped result-returning tools as the one supported live-app observation workflow. Cover the smallest coherent cross-repo seam under `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/**`, the companion `re-frame2-pair.runtime` preload and Pair skill, and the MCP conformance fixtures that pin the public catalogue.

## Findings

- The source catalogue exposes 33 tools. Four are one push-streaming subsystem, and four environment/launch controls exist only to bound that subsystem (`MAX_STREAMS`, event rate, abuse threshold, abuse window). This is a large public and configuration tax for an optional observation route.
- `subscribe` does not return observations as the tool result. It holds `tools/call` open until cancellation/cap/termination, emits useful data through `notifications/progress`, then returns only a terminal summary. Pair-MCP's own live conformance witness must keep a `subscribePromise` open and issue `dispatch` concurrently to exercise it. That is a valid custom MCP-client pattern, but not the natural sequential turn shape of a coding agent; out-of-band `unsubscribe` has the same second-concurrent-call assumption.
- Every normal pairing outcome already has a turn-shaped route: `dispatch` returns its consequence or settled epoch; `trace-window` / `watch-epochs` read bounded history; `watch-until` blocks to a data predicate and returns the sample; `record` + `read-recording` cover human/intermittent interaction; and `tail-build` waits for hot reload. The rare need for a bespoke live listener remains expressible through the default-enabled `eval-cljs` escape hatch and does not justify four permanent public tools.
- Eight dedicated Pair-MCP source/test files (`subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `list-streams`, `get-stream-controls`, `resource-controls`, and their three largest focused suites) already total 3,056 lines / 156,022 bytes, before `resource_controls_test.cljs`, the preload's subscription queues/listener fan-out, server/config plumbing, the long catalogue sections, skill prose, and the dedicated live conformance script are counted.
- The complexity is not passive. The stream needs dual event/byte queue caps, drop-oldest accounting, a token bucket, an abuse window, dead-connection retry/termination, cancellation and out-of-band teardown, per-tick cap/dedup/elision, and two diagnostic tools to explain the controls. History records repeated follow-on repairs for lost events, uncapped progress frames, dead drain loops, privacy projection, frame scoping, and control observability.
- The generated descriptor manifest is already 88,930 bytes for the full catalogue. Removing four host-specialized tools reduces the always-advertised surface as well as implementation weight; retaining them as aliases would preserve the cost and defeat the pre-alpha simplification.

## Recommended Action

Delete `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `list-streams`, and `get-stream-controls` from the registry and remove the streaming-only server/runtime implementation: runtime subscription queues and drain API, polling controller, progress payloads, concurrent-slot/rate/abuse controls, their flags/environment variables, diagnostics, and teardown state. Do not add a generic replacement, deprecated aliases, tombstones, or a compatibility mode.

Rewrite the Pair routing guidance around returned-result workflows:

1. Use `dispatch` consequence/settle for an action the agent initiated.
2. Use `watch-epochs` or `trace-window` for retained event/trace history.
3. Use `watch-until` for a known asynchronous condition.
4. Use `record` + `read-recording` while a human or the browser drives the app.
5. Use `tail-build` for code reload.

Keep `list-subscriptions`: it reads the app's reactive subscription cache and is unrelated to MCP progress streams. Preserve the retained tools' existing privacy projection, elision, wire caps, and explicit time bounds; do not replace deleted stream controls with another permission or resource-control layer.

## Evidence

- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/registry.cljs` registers the four tools as a distinct streaming/diagnostic family.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/subscribe.cljs` is 864 lines. Its contract says the call runs until abort/unsubscribe and carries observations in `notifications/progress`; the final result is a summary. `resource_controls.cljs` adds another 479 lines.
- `tools/mcp-conformance/test/live-re-frame2-pair-subscribe.cjs` explicitly starts `client.callTool(subscribe)` without awaiting it, fires `dispatch` concurrently, accumulates `onprogress` callbacks, and only later awaits the terminal subscription result. The test demonstrates the concurrency contract rather than a normal one-call/one-result agent workflow.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/package.json`, `spec/API.md`, and `spec/003-Tool-Catalogue.md` expose the stream configuration, progress wire shape, caps, filters, diagnostics, and five termination paths.
- `skills/re-frame2-pair/preload/re_frame2_pair/runtime.cljs` owns the streaming queue/listener fan-out (`subscribe!`, `drain-subscription!`, `unsubscribe!`, `subscription-info`) in addition to the retained history and recorder surfaces.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/tool-descriptors.edn` reports 33 tools and is 88,930 bytes; the streaming family consumes four names and their always-loaded descriptions/schemas.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/get_re_frame2_pair_instructions.cljs` already presents `watch-until`, `record`, `subscribe`, and `tail-build` as alternate waiting routes, confirming overlap at the routing layer.
- Source/commit history identifies the additive lineage and its repair tail: rf2-hq49 (push subscribe/unsubscribe), rf2-ho4ve (byte budget), rf2-uvfph (rate-limit event preservation), rf2-a0kxsb / rf2-3ijbl (controls and observability), and rf2-ajhwbm (dead drain-loop termination).

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `list-streams`, and `get-stream-controls` are absent from `registry/tools`, `tools/list`, the canonical tool-name fixture, generated descriptor manifest, conformance corpus, package README/API/catalogue, Pair skill allow-list/routing, and current capability/status docs. No alias, deprecated descriptor, or unknown-tool special case preserves them.
2. Streaming-only Pair-MCP files and code paths are removed. The server has no progress-notification emitter, stream slot/token-bucket/abuse-window state, stream-specific launch flags or environment variables, or stream cleanup branch. The preload has no Pair-owned stream registry, bounded event queue, drain loop API, or stream-only listener fan-out. Shared framework trace/epoch facilities used by retained reads remain intact.
3. `list-subscriptions` remains and is documented/tested as the reactive app subscription-cache read, with no streaming terminology or dependency.
4. A live end-to-end witness proves the retained turn-shaped workflow without concurrent MCP calls: dispatch an event, observe its returned consequence and retained epoch/trace; a focused `watch-until` test returns a matching asynchronous sample; and the existing recorder path still captures and returns a browser/human-driven change. Each observation reaches the agent in a completed tool result, not a progress callback.
5. Tool annotations, schemas, `tool-descriptors.edn`, the stdio catalogue snapshot, and cross-server MCP conformance agree with the reduced surface. The Pair package tests, descriptor-drift check, stdio round trip, and relevant live fixture/conformance lanes pass non-vacuously.
6. Current docs state one observation decision tree using the five retained routes above. Historical design notes may record that push streaming once existed, but no current setup, recipe, status table, or diagnostic ladder instructs an agent to use it.
7. No new public tool, compatibility shim, permission gate, scheduler, queue, or background service is introduced to replace the deleted subsystem.

## Non-goals

- Removing or weakening `read-sub` / `list-subscriptions`, framework trace/epoch listeners, epoch retention, privacy projection, elision, or the ordinary per-response wire cap.
- Redesigning the remaining 29-tool catalogue, globally rewriting descriptor prose, or combining unrelated tools in this change.
- Changing MCP itself, adding a different streaming transport, or supporting dashboard/telemetry clients whose primary workload is continuous event consumption.
- Preserving compatibility for the four removed pre-alpha names, migration aliases, deprecation windows, or launch-flag no-ops.
- Tightening eval/write permissions or adding safety confirmations. The installed local Pair-MCP and explicit invoker remain the trust boundary.

## Related beads

No open or in-progress duplicate was found after title and full-description searches for `subscribe`, `stream`, `notifications/progress`, `push-mode`, `list-streams`, and `resource-control`.

- `rf2-wyza` (closed) removed the duplicated 33-entry onboarding catalogue in favor of routing rules after measuring the permanent tools/list context tax; this is the same pre-alpha/trust-the-agent posture applied to a redundant runtime subsystem.
- `rf2-ov144` (open) is an adjacent Pair-MCP catalogue change for replay-by-epoch-id. It is not a dependency; coordinate registry/manifest edits if both land concurrently.
- Historical implementation lineage retained in source/commits: rf2-hq49, rf2-ho4ve, rf2-uvfph, rf2-a0kxsb, rf2-3ijbl, and rf2-ajhwbm.

DECISION: Option A — the PR #8815 retirement of subscribe, unsubscribe, list-streams and get-stream-controls is RATIFIED as the permanent shape of the Pair-MCP surface. No restore, no aliases, no tombstones, no compatibility mode, no off-by-default flag, no replacement permission/resource-control layer. Confirmed read-only via gh at ruling time: #8815 state MERGED, mergedAt 2026-08-31T19:28:41Z, 104 files, +931/-7538. The ruling changes no schedule: rf2-ov144 keeps building on the 29-tool registry and the in-flight residual worker's scope is unchanged.

Reasoning adopted. The subsystem was wrong-shaped for its only real consumer. A coding agent gets observations in a completed tool result or not at all; subscribe held tools/call open, shipped its data sideways through notifications/progress, and returned only a delivery summary, so exercising it required a second concurrent MCP call (the deleted witness's own unawaited subscribePromise plus a concurrent dispatch). Every observation an agent or programmer actually needs has a turn-shaped route that returns data: dispatch consequence/settle, watch-epochs/trace-window, watch-until, record + read-recording, tail-build. Pre-alpha with no external users is the cheapest possible moment to delete a wrong-shaped public surface, and trust-the-programmer cuts the same way: the rare bespoke listener stays reachable through eval-cljs over re-frame.trace.tooling/register-listener! (verified at tip: implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/tooling.cljc:81) without four permanent public tools, four launch controls and a token bucket standing guard over it.

TASTE FLAG, answered explicitly. The triage flag was: "a shipped capability repaired six times is being deleted." I adopt the run-rate reading, not the sunk-cost reading. The repair tail — 06a1d75df3 rate-gate event loss, 7cd4a4f2f0 uncapped progress tick, b0a524ebb4 launch controls/observability, 62a10dcf36 dead drain-loop termination, d01215a070 per-frame elision, 0f5c17f960 and 54256d52a6 isError envelopes, b9acd02fa9 frame pin not scoping subscribe; eight commits June to August, the dossier's seven and the reviewer's one extra taken together — is the measured carrying cost of a concurrency-heavy push pipe that no default workflow used. Each repair was sensible, because a real stream needs queue budgets, rate limiting, teardown, backpressure accounting, privacy projection and observability; that is exactly why keeping it means keeping that ownership burden. "It finally works" was equally true of the 33-entry onboarding catalogue rf2-wyza removed after measuring its context tax; this is the same posture one layer down. The investment is not honoured by carrying the thing forward; it is honoured by the whole subsystem sitting in git history at 89bb4d49f1^, restorable deliberately, as a decision, if a real consumer ever appears.

HOW THE OPINIONS WERE WEIGHED. Two voices in the dossier: the original author (sections "Summary" through "Evidence") and one reviewer ("Codex Recommendation"). Both recommend Option A; the reviewer states its conclusion "does not depend on the bead's analysis" and re-derives it from the deleted implementation and witness, the installed SDK, and the protocol text.

Agreements, adopted: ratify as merged; no aliases/tombstones/flag/subscribe-only; the concurrent-call contract is the decisive product-fit defect; the retained five routes are coherent and each has a focused suite plus the live turn-observation witness; the recorder-arm false-green is a test-causality defect in a retained route and gives no reason to restore streaming; list-subscriptions stays (it reads the app's reactive sub-cache and has nothing to do with MCP streams).

Disagreement, and the REVIEWER WINS it: the author wrote "Nothing an agent or programmer does today is lost" and framed the loss as only "a dashboard- or telemetry-style consumer". The reviewer corrects the framing: there IS a real loss. The retained tools do not reproduce a low-latency continuous feed, progress-callback delivery, or the old raw/frameless trace topic; polling can miss records after ring rollover and costs extra calls; eval-cljs is raw, not an equivalent structured, privacy-projected API. The correct claim is therefore "that unique capability has no demonstrated consumer in Pair-MCP's supported model-facing workflow", not "streaming had no unique capability". I adopt the reviewer's wording as the ruling's claim. It changes nothing about the decision — the bead's non-goals already rule that client class out of scope — but the record must not overstate.

Reviewer additions adopted: the REOPEN CRITERIA, all four of which must hold before the streaming question is reopened — (i) a concrete client that can consume callbacks concurrently and surface them usefully to its model or UI; (ii) retained history/recording measured as unable to meet a stated latency or loss requirement; (iii) the missing topic, frameless events included, specified; (iv) an owner accepting the queue, privacy, reconnect, rate-limit and conformance matrix. THE DOCUMENTED DECISION TREE — the five returned-result routes that current docs state as the ONE observation workflow (AC6), each a completed tool result with no concurrent calls:
1. An action the agent initiated -> dispatch: returns :epoch-id, :db-changed?, :changed-paths, :effects-fired, :no-op?, :cascade-summary; with settle true one call returns the settled epoch including its render events.
2. Retained history -> watch-epochs {:since-id N :pred ...} (pull-mode poll of epochs after an id) or trace-window {:window-ms N} (diff-encoded records from the last N ms).
3. A known asynchronous condition -> watch-until: blocks server-side on a signal predicate and returns the matching sample (or the last sample on timeout).
4. A human or the browser driving the app -> record (read-only per-rAF observer with a stop condition, returns :recording-id immediately) + read-recording {:drain true} incrementally, or {:stop true} to read and close. This is what the long-session streaming case reduces to.
5. Code reload -> tail-build: polls a probe form against a pre-edit baseline until the hot reload lands.
Bespoke live listener: eval-cljs over re-frame.trace.tooling/register-listener!. list-subscriptions stays, documented as the app's reactive sub-cache read with no streaming terminology.

MUST NOT be added back, under this bead or any follow-up: the four names in any form (alias, deprecated descriptor, unknown-tool special case, tombstone); a compatibility or --enable-streams mode; launch-flag no-ops for --max-concurrent-streams, --max-events-per-sec, --abuse-overflow-threshold, --abuse-window-ms or RE_FRAME2_PAIR_MCP_MAX_STREAMS; a replacement permission gate, scheduler, queue, background service or resource-control layer; a new public tool standing in for streaming. Retained tools keep their existing privacy projection, elision, wire caps and explicit time bounds untouched.
